title: The star cluster NGC 3766

celestial: NGC 3766 · constellation Centaurus · about 7000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: These young stars make up NGC 3766, an open star cluster, in the constellation Centaurus, the Centaur. ESO's MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile took the picture.

An open cluster is a loose family of stars born together from the same cloud of gas, so its members share a similar age and origin. That makes clusters like this a useful place to compare stars that started out under the same conditions.

NGC 3766 has turned out to hold a surprise. A team from the Geneva Observatory watched its stars very carefully with the Swiss 1.2-meter Leonhard Euler Telescope, also at La Silla, and found that 36 of them belong to a new and previously unknown class of variable star. Variable stars are stars whose brightness changes over time, and each class tells astronomers something different about what goes on inside them.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (25.00 x 23.98 arcminutes) and distance (7000 light years), the frame spans roughly 51 × 49 light-years. Its light set out about 7,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope combines B, V and I filters, spanning visible light into the near-infrared. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and the subtle brightness changes of variable stars can only be found with careful measurements over time.
